subtopic_detail: Persistent yearning and preoccupation with a deceased spouse fourteen months after the death with preserved self worth and no pervasive anhedonia
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68 year old woman fourteen months after her husband died. She says she thinks about him almost all day, sets his place at the table, has not been able to give away his clothes, and finds it hard to believe he is really gone.

She has stopped seeing the friends they had as a couple because being with them is unbearable, but she still enjoys her grandchildren and her garden, eats normally and does not feel worthless. She has no thoughts of ending her life and says she wants to feel able to live again.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when speaking about her husband and brightens when discussing her grandchildren, no psychomotor retardation, speech normal in rate and volume, no perceptual disturbance, cognition intact on brief testing, weight stable
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid stimulating hormone and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start an antidepressant and review the response after four to six weeks
options.rationale: Antidepressants are indicated where a depressive episode coexists, which is identified by pervasive anhedonia, worthlessness, guilt unrelated to the death and diurnal variation. Her enjoyment of her grandchildren and preserved self worth argue against that, and trials of antidepressants for grief specific symptoms have been disappointing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a benzodiazepine for sleep and emotional distress
options.rationale: Sedatives blunt the emotional processing that grief work depends on and carry dependence and falls risk in an older adult. Their use in early bereavement is associated with worse rather than better outcomes at follow up. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Advise that this is expected after a long marriage and review her in six months
options.rationale: Normalising grief is the right approach in the first months and for most bereaved people throughout. Symptoms this intense and this disabling more than a year after the death fall outside the expected trajectory, and further watchful waiting has not helped her over the past year. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer for a structured grief focused psychological therapy with planned review
options.rationale: Intense yearning and preoccupation with avoidance, disbelief and identity disruption persisting beyond twelve months with functional impairment describes prolonged grief disorder, which affects roughly one in ten bereaved people and does not resolve with time alone. Grief focused psychotherapy, which combines exposure to the reality of the loss with restoration of life goals, outperforms both generic supportive counselling and antidepressants for these symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer to a bereavement support group as the sole intervention for her symptoms
options.rationale: Peer support groups help many bereaved people and are a reasonable adjunct that she may value. Randomised evidence shows generic support does not reduce prolonged grief symptoms in those who meet criteria, who need a targeted therapy instead. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Grief is a normal response to loss and most bereaved people adapt without professional intervention, so the clinical task is identifying the minority whose grief becomes persistent and disabling. Prolonged grief disorder is now a formal diagnosis requiring symptoms at least twelve months after the death in adults, with intense yearning or preoccupation plus features such as disbelief, avoidance of reminders, emotional numbness, identity disruption and an inability to re engage with life. It is distinguished from a depressive episode, in which low mood is pervasive rather than focused on the deceased, self worth is reduced and anhedonia is global, although the two frequently coexist. Treatment is psychological and specifically grief focused, with medication reserved for a comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder rather than for the grief itself.
key_points: Diagnosis requires symptoms persisting at least twelve months after the death
Yearning and preoccupation focus on the deceased rather than on global low mood
Preserved self worth and selective enjoyment argue against a depressive episode
Grief focused psychotherapy outperforms generic support and antidepressants
Medication is reserved for comorbid depressive or anxiety disorder
explanation.pearls: Bereavement by suicide, homicide or sudden unexpected death, and the loss of a child, carry the highest risk of prolonged grief disorder, so those groups warrant proactive follow up at around six to twelve months rather than waiting for presentation.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Adolescent using a nicotine vaping device hourly with morning use and failed unassisted quit attempts
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 16 year old boy who asks for help stopping vaping. He tells you he uses a disposable device roughly every hour, reaches for it within fifteen minutes of waking, and gets irritable and unable to concentrate in class when he cannot use it.

He has tried three times to stop on his own and lasted at most two days each time. He has never smoked cigarettes, uses no other drugs, has no respiratory or cardiac history, and is attending school and doing reasonably well.

data_table.Examination: Chest clear with no wheeze, no cyanosis or clubbing, mental state examination shows no depressive or psychotic features, engaged and motivated in the consultation

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise abrupt cessation with a written quit date and review in one month
options.rationale: Setting a quit date is part of any cessation plan and is worth doing, but advice alone is what has already failed on three occasions. Dependence of this severity predicts withdrawal that undermines unassisted attempts. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation

options.text: Prescribe varenicline with weekly telephone contact through the quit attempt
options.rationale: Varenicline is an effective first line agent for nicotine dependence in adults and would be a reasonable choice were he older. It is not approved for use under 18 years and safety and efficacy data in adolescents are lacking. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation

options.text: Offer behavioural support with nicotine replacement therapy and structured follow up
options.rationale: Waking use within fifteen minutes, hourly use and withdrawal symptoms on abstinence indicate significant nicotine dependence, for which behavioural support combined with nicotine replacement is the recommended approach in an adolescent who has failed unassisted attempts. Combination replacement, using a patch for background craving with a short acting form for breakthrough, is more effective than either alone, and structured follow up in the first weeks is when relapse is most likely. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation

options.text: Advise switching to a lower nicotine concentration device and gradual reduction
options.rationale: Tapering the concentration appears logical but users compensate by inhaling more deeply and more often, so actual nicotine intake changes little. It also keeps the behavioural ritual of the device intact, which is a major driver of relapse. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation

options.text: Refer to a specialist drug and alcohol service and defer treatment until assessed
options.rationale: Specialist referral is warranted for polysubstance use, significant comorbid mental illness or repeated failure of primary care management, none of which apply to a motivated adolescent at his first assisted attempt. Deferring treatment risks losing a window in which he is ready to act. (Source: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation)
source_refs: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation

explanation.summary: Nicotine vaping among Australian adolescents rose steeply before regulatory tightening, and many users are dependent without ever having smoked a cigarette, which reverses the historical assumption that vaping is a downstream problem of smoking. Dependence is assessed as it is for tobacco, with time to first use after waking, daily frequency and withdrawal symptoms being the most informative questions. Nicotine replacement therapy is used in dependent adolescents despite being formally studied mainly in adults, because the risks of continued nicotine exposure during brain development outweigh the risks of short term replacement. Varenicline and bupropion are not recommended under 18 years, and behavioural support, whether delivered in the consultation or through quit services, roughly doubles the chance of success when combined with pharmacotherapy.
key_points: Many adolescent users are nicotine dependent without prior cigarette smoking
Time to first use after waking is a key marker of dependence severity
Combination nicotine replacement outperforms a single form
Varenicline and bupropion are not recommended under 18 years
Behavioural support combined with pharmacotherapy doubles quit rates
explanation.pearls: Nicotine withdrawal peaks within the first three days and largely settles by two to four weeks, so scheduling review inside that window rather than at one month is what catches the relapse most attempts fail at.

sources.label: RACGP: Supporting smoking and vaping cessation

subtopic_detail: Young adult with irresistible daytime sleep episodes and sudden bilateral leg weakness triggered by laughter with retained awareness
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 22 year old apprentice referred by his employer after falling asleep at a workbench. He says he cannot stay awake through the afternoon no matter how much he sleeps at night, and that a ten minute nap leaves him refreshed for a couple of hours.

His girlfriend has seen him sag at the knees and slump forward when he laughs hard, lasting under a minute, and he says he can hear everything while it happens and is not confused afterwards. He sometimes wakes unable to move for a few seconds and occasionally sees figures in the room as he falls asleep.

data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23 kg/m2, no goitre, cranial nerves and peripheral neurological examination normal, no proximal weakness, reflexes present and symmetrical, mental state examination shows no depressive features, oropharynx unobstructed with a Mallampati score of 1
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, iron studies, electrolytes, thyroid stimulating hormone and glucose all within normal limits, Epworth Sleepiness Scale 19

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Arrange an electroencephalogram to investigate probable atonic seizures
options.rationale: Atonic seizures cause abrupt loss of tone with impaired awareness and frequently with injury and postictal confusion. His episodes are emotionally triggered, awareness is fully retained throughout and there is no postictal phase, which is not the pattern of a seizure. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Advise sleep hygiene measures and a regular bedtime and review in two months
options.rationale: Insufficient sleep syndrome is the commonest cause of daytime sleepiness in young adults and does respond to scheduling, so this is a reasonable starting point in most presentations. It does not explain emotionally triggered loss of muscle tone, which has a narrow differential. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Start a modafinil trial and assess the response to treatment after four weeks
options.rationale: Wake promoting agents are a mainstay of treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed, so the drug itself is appropriate to the condition. Starting it before objective testing removes the ability to perform a valid multiple sleep latency test later and leaves the diagnosis unconfirmed for life. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Refer for psychiatric assessment of possible functional neurological symptoms
options.rationale: Functional collapse attacks are worth considering when episodes are prolonged, variable and inconsistent with any physiological pattern. Stereotyped brief emotionally triggered atonia with retained awareness, alongside sleep paralysis and hallucinations at sleep onset, forms a recognised physiological cluster. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy)

options.text: Refer to a sleep physician for overnight polysomnography and daytime nap testing
options.rationale: Excessive daytime sleepiness with refreshing short naps, sleep paralysis, hypnagogic hallucinations and emotionally triggered loss of tone with retained awareness is narcolepsy with cataplexy, which is confirmed by overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test the next day. The overnight study is required both to exclude another cause of sleep disruption and to validate the nap test, which looks for a short mean sleep latency with early entry into rapid eye movement sleep. (Source: Australasian Sleep Association: Narcolepsy)

explanation.summary: Narcolepsy type 1 results from loss of hypocretin producing neurons in the lateral hypothalamus and typically begins in adolescence or early adulthood, with a diagnostic delay often measured in years because sleepiness is attributed to lifestyle. The defining feature is cataplexy, a brief emotionally triggered loss of muscle tone with fully retained awareness, which represents intrusion of rapid eye movement sleep atonia into wakefulness and is what separates the condition from other causes of hypersomnolence. Other rapid eye movement intrusion phenomena, namely sleep paralysis and hallucinations at sleep onset or waking, support the diagnosis but are not specific and occur in the general population. Diagnosis requires overnight polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test, and because stimulants and antidepressants alter both studies they must be withheld beforehand. Management combines scheduled naps, a wake promoting agent for sleepiness, an agent suppressing rapid eye movement sleep for cataplexy, and mandatory discussion of driving and occupational safety.
key_points: Cataplexy is emotionally triggered atonia with fully retained awareness
Short naps that refresh distinguish it from most other causes of sleepiness
Diagnosis requires polysomnography followed by a multiple sleep latency test
Stimulants and antidepressants must be withheld before testing
Driving and occupational safety must be addressed at diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Antidepressants suppress rapid eye movement sleep and can abolish the early rapid eye movement periods that the multiple sleep latency test depends on, so they are withdrawn for at least two weeks before testing or the study will be falsely negative.

subtopic_detail: Evening leg discomfort relieved by walking with an iron store at the low end of the population range and no anaemia
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 54 year old woman who describes a crawling, creeping discomfort deep in both calves that starts when she sits down after dinner and builds until she has to get up and walk. Walking relieves it within a minute and it returns when she sits again.

It is worst between 9 pm and midnight and it takes her more than an hour to fall asleep most nights. Her partner says her legs jerk repeatedly once she is asleep. She takes no regular medication and her periods stopped four years ago.

data_table.Examination: Calves non tender with no swelling or varicosities, pedal pulses present, no sensory loss to light touch or pinprick, ankle reflexes present, straight leg raise negative bilaterally, no skin changes
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 129 g/L (115 to 155), mean cell volume 88 fL (80 to 100), ferritin 32 micrograms/L (30 to 300), transferrin saturation 16 percent (15 to 45), estimated glomerular filtration rate 88 mL/min/1.73m2 (greater than 60), thyroid stimulating hormone 1.7 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), glucose 4.9 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4), vitamin B12 372 pmol/L (150 to 700)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Start a dopamine agonist at a low dose and titrate to symptom control
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists relieve symptoms quickly and were first line for many years, which is why they remain a tempting choice. Long term use causes augmentation, in which symptoms become earlier, more intense and spread to the arms, and this is now considered severe enough that these agents are no longer recommended first. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start oral iron replacement and reassess symptoms and iron stores after three months
options.rationale: Brain iron deficiency underlies the dopaminergic dysfunction of this condition, and iron replacement is recommended when ferritin is at or below 75 micrograms/L or transferrin saturation is under 20 percent, both of which apply here despite the absence of anaemia. Correcting stores improves or resolves symptoms in a substantial proportion and avoids committing her to a drug with long term complications. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start an alpha 2 delta ligand at night and titrate the dose to effect
options.rationale: Alpha 2 delta ligands such as gabapentin or pregabalin are the preferred pharmacological agents when drug treatment is needed, particularly with coexisting pain or insomnia. They are reserved until reversible contributors have been corrected, because treating over an uncorrected iron deficiency commits the patient to indefinite therapy. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Start a low dose benzodiazepine at night to improve her sleep onset latency
options.rationale: Hypnotics may mask the sleep disturbance but do nothing for the sensory urge to move, which is the core symptom. They also carry tolerance, dependence and falls risk with indefinite use in middle and later life. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies before committing to any specific treatment
options.rationale: Neurophysiology is indicated where a peripheral neuropathy is suspected from sensory loss, absent reflexes or a length dependent distribution, none of which are present. The circadian pattern and relief by movement are not features of neuropathy and do not require electrophysiology. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Neurology)

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome is a clinical diagnosis resting on an urge to move the legs with unpleasant sensations, worsening at rest, relief by movement and a circadian pattern peaking in the evening and night, with other causes excluded. Periodic limb movements in sleep accompany it in most affected people and are often what the bed partner reports. Assessment focuses on reversible contributors, principally iron deficiency, renal impairment, pregnancy and drugs including antihistamines, dopamine antagonists and most antidepressants. The threshold for iron replacement is set far higher than the threshold for diagnosing anaemia, because brain iron can be deficient when peripheral stores look acceptable. When drug treatment is needed, alpha 2 delta ligands have displaced dopamine agonists as first line because of augmentation, which is a paradoxical worsening that is difficult to reverse once established.
key_points: Diagnosis is clinical, requiring rest worsening, movement relief and a circadian pattern
Iron replacement is indicated at ferritin 75 micrograms/L or below
Anaemia is not required for iron deficiency to be driving symptoms
Alpha 2 delta ligands are preferred over dopamine agonists when drugs are needed
Antihistamines, dopamine antagonists and most antidepressants aggravate it
explanation.pearls: Augmentation from a dopamine agonist announces itself as symptoms starting earlier in the day, becoming more intense, or spreading to the arms, and the correct response is to withdraw the agonist rather than to increase the dose.

sources.label: Australasian Sleep Association: Restless legs syndrome

subtopic_detail: Adult woman with lifelong social exhaustion and rigid routines who has carried several psychiatric labels without sustained response to treatment
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 34 year old woman who brings a list of questions and asks whether she might be autistic, having recognised herself in an account written by another woman.

She describes rehearsing conversations beforehand, copying colleagues' phrases, and needing to lie in a dark room for hours after social events. She has eaten the same lunch daily for eleven years, is distressed by unexpected changes to plans, and has intense long standing interests in textile history. She has been treated for social anxiety and for depression over fifteen years with partial and short lived benefit. She works, has one close friend, and made eye contact throughout, which she tells you she finds effortful and has practised.

data_table.Examination: Mental state examination shows no current depressive episode, no psychotic features and no current suicidal ideation, speech normal in form, insight good, no evidence of an eating disorder with a body mass index of 22 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, thyroid stimulating hormone and vitamin B12 all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase her antidepressant dose and review the response after six weeks
options.rationale: Dose escalation is appropriate for a partially treated depressive or anxiety disorder that is otherwise well characterised. Fifteen years of partial and short lived response to treatments for two different diagnoses is itself a reason to revisit the formulation rather than to intensify treatment of it. (Source: RACGP: Autism in adults)

options.text: Reassure her that autism is unlikely given her employment and eye contact
options.rationale: Employment, friendship and eye contact are frequently cited to exclude autism in adult women and none of them do so. She has explicitly described learned eye contact, and camouflaging of this kind is a major reason women are identified late or not at all. (Source: RACGP: Autism in adults)

options.text: Refer for a specialist diagnostic assessment with a developmental history
options.rationale: Lifelong social effort and camouflaging, sensory overload requiring recovery, insistence on sameness and circumscribed intense interests, combined with a long history of psychiatric labels that responded only partially, is a characteristic presentation of an undiagnosed autistic adult woman. Diagnosis in Australia requires a specialist multidisciplinary or specialist clinician assessment that includes a developmental history from childhood, since it cannot be made from current presentation alone. (Source: RACGP: Autism in adults)

options.text: Administer a self report autism screening questionnaire and act on the score
options.rationale: Screening questionnaires are useful for deciding whether to refer and she would almost certainly score above threshold. They are not diagnostic, cannot capture the childhood history that diagnosis requires, and a score alone will not give her access to supports. (Source: RACGP: Autism in adults)

options.text: Refer for personality disorder assessment given the chronic interpersonal pattern
options.rationale: Personality disorder is a genuine differential and autistic women are commonly given that label, particularly borderline personality disorder, because of emotional dysregulation and unstable relationships. Her difficulties are consistent since early childhood, are driven by sensory and social processing rather than by fear of abandonment or identity disturbance, and do not fluctuate with interpersonal events. (Source: RACGP: Autism in adults)

explanation.summary: Autism is substantially under recognised in women and girls, who are diagnosed later and less often than males with comparable needs, in large part because diagnostic constructs were derived from male presentations. Camouflaging, meaning the conscious or learned masking of autistic traits through rehearsed conversation, imitation and forced eye contact, is more common in women and is effortful enough to be a driver of exhaustion, anxiety and depression. Special interests in autistic women are often socially acceptable in content, such as animals, literature or a historical subject, which means they are not recognised as unusual in intensity. The typical history is of serial psychiatric diagnoses with partial treatment response, and formal diagnosis frequently reframes a lifetime of self blame while opening access to supports and workplace adjustments.
key_points: Autistic women are diagnosed later and less often than men with similar needs
Camouflaging can produce apparently normal eye contact and social performance
Interests may be socially typical in content but atypical in intensity
Serial psychiatric labels with partial response is a characteristic history
Diagnosis requires specialist assessment including a developmental history
explanation.pearls: Autistic burnout, a period of profound exhaustion, loss of skills and reduced tolerance to stimulus after prolonged camouflaging, is frequently misdiagnosed and treated as a depressive episode, and it responds to reduced demands and sensory recovery rather than to antidepressant escalation.

sources.label: Autism CRC: National guideline for the assessment and diagnosis of autism in Australia

subtopic_detail: Persistent sense of watching oneself from outside and of surroundings appearing unreal beginning after a cannabis episode with intact reality testing
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 21 year old university student who says that for the past seven months he has felt as though he is watching himself from a few feet away and that the world looks flat, as if through glass. He is frightened that he is going mad.

It began during an episode of intense anxiety after using a high potency cannabis product at a party, and has continued daily since although he has not used cannabis or any other drug since that night. He knows the feeling is not real and says nothing has actually changed about the room or about him, and he has no hallucinations and no unusual beliefs.

data_table.Examination: Anxious and pressured when describing the symptom, oriented with intact attention and memory, no perceptual abnormality elicited, no delusional beliefs, insight fully retained, no depressive episode, neurological examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid stimulating hormone and urine drug screen all unremarkable

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Start an antipsychotic at a low dose and review the response in four weeks
options.rationale: Antipsychotics treat psychosis, which requires loss of reality testing through hallucinations or delusions. He knows the experience is not real, which is the defining distinction, and antipsychotics have not been shown to help these symptoms. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe a regular benzodiazepine to reduce the anxiety driving the experience
options.rationale: Short term anxiolysis may seem attractive given how frightening the symptom is, and anxiety genuinely amplifies it. Regular benzodiazepine use promotes dependence and, on withdrawal, characteristically intensifies these experiences, so the net effect over months is harmful. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging of the brain before offering any treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated where the experience is accompanied by focal neurological signs, an altered level of consciousness, olfactory or gustatory phenomena or stereotyped brief episodes suggesting temporal lobe seizures. A continuous seven month experience with a normal neurological examination and intact cognition does not fit that pattern. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure him that this resolves without treatment and review him in six months
options.rationale: Many episodes triggered by intoxication or acute stress do settle within days to weeks, so watchful waiting is reasonable early on. Seven months of continuous daily symptoms with significant distress has already declared itself as persistent rather than transient. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Explain the diagnosis and refer for psychological therapy with planned review
options.rationale: Persistent detachment from oneself or from surroundings with fully intact reality testing, in the absence of another disorder or substance effect, is depersonalisation derealisation disorder, and cannabis is one of its commonest precipitants. Explanation that the experience is a recognised and non psychotic phenomenon substantially reduces the catastrophic fear that maintains it, and psychological therapy targeting symptom monitoring, catastrophic appraisal and avoidance is the treatment with the best evidence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Depersonalisation is the experience of detachment from one's own body, thoughts or actions, and derealisation the sense that surroundings are unreal, dreamlike or visually flattened, and brief episodes occur in up to half the general population under stress, fatigue or intoxication. The disorder is diagnosed when the experience is persistent or recurrent, causes distress or impairment, and occurs with fully preserved reality testing, which is the feature that separates it from psychosis and is the single most useful question to ask. It commonly follows acute anxiety, cannabis or hallucinogen use, or severe stress, and a self reinforcing cycle develops in which the fear of going mad amplifies the detachment. Assessment excludes temporal lobe epilepsy, migraine aura, substance effects and the dissociation of post traumatic stress disorder, and management is psychoeducation plus psychological therapy, since no medication has established efficacy.
key_points: Reality testing is intact, which distinguishes it from psychosis
Cannabis, acute anxiety and severe stress are common precipitants
Fear of going mad maintains and amplifies the symptom
Exclude temporal lobe epilepsy, migraine aura and substance effects
Psychoeducation and psychological therapy have the best evidence
explanation.pearls: Asking directly whether the person believes things really have changed, or only feels as though they have, separates this disorder from psychosis in a single question, and the answer is diagnostic in a way that no investigation is.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for anxiety disorders

subtopic_detail: Inner restlessness and constant pacing appearing days after an antipsychotic dose increase with resolving delusions and no tremor or rigidity
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 24 year old man admitted eleven days ago with a first episode of psychosis. His risperidone was increased four days ago and since then the nurses report he cannot settle, paces the corridor from early morning, and stands up and sits down repeatedly through meals.

He tells you he no longer believes the neighbours are transmitting to him and that the voices have almost stopped, but that he feels a dreadful churning inside his legs that only walking eases, and that he would rather be dead than feel like this for another week. He is sleeping about three hours a night.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92 beats per minute, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 percent on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Constantly shifting weight from foot to foot when standing and crossing and uncrossing his legs when seated, no resting tremor, no cogwheel rigidity, no abnormal involuntary movements of the face or tongue, no myoclonus, no hyperreflexia, oriented with normal cognition, mental state examination shows resolving delusions and reduced auditory hallucinations
data_table.Investigations: Creatine kinase 130 U/L (less than 200), electrolytes and renal function within normal limits, thyroid stimulating hormone 1.4 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), urine drug screen negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reduce the antipsychotic dose and add propranolol with close observation
options.rationale: Subjective inner restlessness with an objective inability to remain still, appearing days after a dose increase and without rigidity, tremor or fever, is akathisia, and the psychotic symptoms are improving rather than worsening. Management is to reduce the offending dose or switch agent, with propranolol as the best supported pharmacological adjunct, and close observation is essential because akathisia carries a recognised association with suicidal thoughts of exactly the kind he has voiced. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Increase the antipsychotic dose further to settle his agitation and improve sleep
options.rationale: Escalation is the intuitive response to a pacing, sleepless patient on a psychiatric ward and is the central trap here, because akathisia is readily misread as psychotic agitation. Increasing the dose worsens the very mechanism causing his distress, and his delusions and hallucinations are in fact receding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add benztropine regularly and review the movement disorder in 48 hours
options.rationale: Anticholinergic agents are effective for acute dystonia and for drug induced parkinsonism, which present with sustained abnormal postures or with tremor and cogwheel rigidity. Their benefit in akathisia is poor, and they add cognitive impairment and constipation without addressing the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Cease the antipsychotic immediately and commence supportive care with cooling
options.rationale: Abrupt cessation with supportive management is the response to neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which requires fever, rigidity, autonomic instability, altered consciousness and a raised creatine kinase. He is afebrile with a normal creatine kinase, normal cognition and no rigidity, and stopping treatment outright risks relapse of a psychosis that is responding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Add a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor for the emerging depressive symptoms
options.rationale: Post psychotic depression is a real phenomenon and his statement about being better off dead makes mood a legitimate concern to assess. His distress is explicitly tied to a physical sensation relieved by walking rather than to pervasive low mood, and some antidepressants can themselves induce or worsen akathisia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Akathisia is a movement disorder combining a subjective sense of inner restlessness, usually referred to the legs, with an objective inability to remain still, and it typically emerges within days to weeks of starting or increasing a dopamine antagonist. It is the extrapyramidal syndrome most often missed, because pacing and sleeplessness in a psychotic patient are easily attributed to the illness, and the resulting dose increase produces a cycle of worsening. The distinguishing features from psychotic agitation are that the patient can describe a physical sensation relieved by movement, and that other psychotic symptoms are stable or improving. Akathisia matters beyond discomfort because it is associated with treatment non adherence and with suicidal ideation and completed suicide, and management centres on reducing or switching the causative agent, with propranolol the best supported adjunct and a benzodiazepine sometimes used short term.
key_points: Subjective inner restlessness plus objective inability to sit still defines it
Onset follows starting or increasing a dopamine antagonist within days to weeks
Improving psychotic symptoms argue against agitation from the illness
Anticholinergics help dystonia and parkinsonism, not akathisia
It carries a recognised association with suicidal ideation and suicide
explanation.pearls: Asking whether the restlessness is felt in the body and eased by moving, rather than felt in the mind, separates akathisia from psychotic agitation at the bedside, and a patient who paces but reports no inner urge usually has something else.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for schizophrenia

subtopic_detail: Older adult becoming confused and unsteady three weeks after starting an antidepressant with a low sodium and concentrated urine
stem:
You are the general practitioner called to see a 79 year old woman at her daughter's request. Three weeks ago you started her on sertraline for a moderate depressive episode after her husband moved into residential care.

Her daughter says her mood is no better and that over the past four days she has become muddled about the day of the week, twice could not find the bathroom in her own home, and has been unsteady on her feet with one near fall. She has had no fever, no cough, no urinary symptoms and no vomiting or diarrhoea, and she is drinking her usual amount. She takes hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension, which she has taken unchanged for nine years.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78 beats per minute, blood pressure 132/78 mmHg lying with no postural drop, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, SpO2 97 percent on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable and oriented to person only, mucous membranes moist with normal skin turgor, jugular venous pressure not elevated, no peripheral oedema, chest clear, abdomen soft, no focal neurological deficit, gait unsteady with a broad base, Abbreviated Mental Test Score 5 out of 10 compared with 10 out of 10 four months ago
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 118 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.2), urea 3.1 mmol/L (3.0 to 8.0), creatinine 62 micromol/L (45 to 90), serum osmolality 248 mOsm/kg (275 to 295), urine osmolality 468 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 52 mmol/L, thyroid stimulating hormone 2.0 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), morning cortisol within normal limits, glucose 5.2 mmol/L (3.0 to 5.4), midstream urine culture no growth, chest radiograph clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Continue the antidepressant and add an antipsychotic for the confusion
options.rationale: Antipsychotics are used for distressing hyperactive delirium once reversible causes are being treated, so they have a place but not as the first action. Adding one here leaves the cause uncorrected and risks further falls and sedation in an older woman who is already unsteady. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Commence intravenous normal saline at a rate to correct the sodium over 24 hours
options.rationale: Isotonic saline is the treatment for hypovolaemic hyponatraemia, identified by dry mucous membranes, postural hypotension, a raised urea and a low urine sodium. With euvolaemia and a urine sodium of 52 mmol/L, saline is often excreted with the sodium retained in the urine and the plasma sodium can paradoxically fall further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Reduce the antidepressant dose by half and repeat the electrolytes in one week
options.rationale: Dose reduction may be adequate for mild asymptomatic hyponatraemia detected on routine monitoring. A sodium of 118 mmol/L with confusion and unsteadiness is symptomatic and carries seizure risk, so partial measures and a week of waiting are unsafe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Cease the antidepressant and refer for admission with fluid restriction and monitoring
options.rationale: A euvolaemic patient with a low serum osmolality, inappropriately concentrated urine and a urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, with normal thyroid and adrenal function, has the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, and the serotonergic antidepressant started three weeks ago is the precipitant in an older woman already taking a thiazide. Treatment is to withdraw the causative drug and restrict fluid with monitored correction, which needs inpatient care at this sodium level because correcting faster than roughly 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours risks osmotic demyelination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

options.text: Arrange computed tomography of the brain and review once the result is available
options.rationale: Neuroimaging is warranted for confusion with focal neurological signs, a history of head injury or anticoagulation, none of which are present. It would be reasonable later if confusion persisted after the sodium was corrected, but it does not address a metabolic cause that is already identified. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endocrinology)

explanation.summary: Selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors are among the commonest drug causes of the syndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis, with risk concentrated in the first weeks of treatment and in older people, low body weight, female sex and concurrent diuretic use. The presentation is easily mistaken for either a worsening of the depression being treated or for an emerging dementia, because it produces lethargy, confusion, unsteadiness and falls rather than anything that points to sodium. Diagnosis requires a clinically euvolaemic patient with low serum osmolality, urine osmolality inappropriately high for that, urine sodium above 30 mmol/L, and exclusion of hypothyroidism, adrenal insufficiency and diuretic effect. Correction is deliberately slow, since raising the sodium faster than about 8 to 10 mmol/L per day risks osmotic demyelination, a devastating and irreversible complication.
key_points: Risk is highest in the first weeks and in older patients on a diuretic
Confusion and falls, not thirst or oedema, are the usual presentation
Euvolaemia with low serum and high urine osmolality defines the syndrome
Thyroid and adrenal function must be normal before the diagnosis is made
Correction is limited to about 8 to 10 mmol/L in 24 hours
explanation.pearls: Checking sodium two to four weeks after starting a serotonergic antidepressant in anyone over 65, particularly those on a thiazide, detects this while it is still asymptomatic and is the single most useful monitoring step in that group.

subtopic_detail: First episode of persistent low mood in a woman with irregular cycles and night sweats who attributes everything to her hormones
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 49 year old accountant who says she is sure her hormones are to blame and wants hormone therapy. Her cycles have become unpredictable over eighteen months, ranging from 21 to 60 days, and she wakes drenched two or three nights a week.

For the past three months she has had low mood every day, has lost interest in things she used to enjoy including her choir, wakes at four each morning, has lost 5 kg without trying and describes herself as a burden to her family. She is making errors at work she would never previously have made. She has never had a depressive episode before and has no thoughts of self harm.

data_table.Examination: Psychomotor retardation with slowed speech and delayed responses, restricted affect, no psychotic features, cognition grossly intact with subjective poor concentration, body mass index 23 kg/m2
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, calcium, thyroid stimulating hormone, vitamin B12 and ferritin all within normal limits, urine pregnancy test negative

lead_in: What would you recommend as initial treatment?

options.text: Menopausal hormone therapy alone with review of her mood in three months
options.rationale: Oestrogen therapy has reasonable evidence for depressive symptoms arising in perimenopause, and it will help her vasomotor symptoms, so it is a legitimate part of her care. It has not been shown to treat a major depressive episode of this severity, and relying on it alone leaves a functionally impairing illness untreated for three months. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause

options.text: Measure follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol and treat according to the result
options.rationale: Gonadotrophin measurement is useful for diagnosing premature ovarian insufficiency under 40 years, and for women without a uterus or on hormonal contraception where cycles cannot be tracked. In a woman of 49 with irregular cycles and vasomotor symptoms the perimenopausal diagnosis is clinical, and fluctuating levels do not guide treatment. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause

options.text: An antidepressant with psychological therapy, and discuss hormone therapy as well
options.rationale: Daily anhedonia for three months with early morning waking, 5 kg of unintentional weight loss, psychomotor retardation, worthlessness and functional decline at work meets criteria for a moderate to severe depressive episode, which is treated on its own terms regardless of the hormonal context. The perimenopausal diagnosis is not in doubt and hormone therapy remains appropriate for her vasomotor symptoms and may assist mood, so it is discussed alongside rather than instead of the antidepressant and therapy. (Source: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause)
source_refs: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause

options.text: Psychological therapy alone with a review of her progress after six weeks
options.rationale: Psychological therapy alone is appropriate for mild to moderate depression and for patients who prefer it, and it should form part of her treatment. Marked biological features with functional impairment at work place this episode in a range where combined treatment gives better and faster outcomes. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Recommend exercise, sleep scheduling and reduced alcohol and review in six weeks
options.rationale: Lifestyle measures improve both vasomotor symptoms and mood and are recommended alongside any treatment, so they belong in the plan. As sole management of a moderate to severe episode with weight loss and impaired work performance they are inadequate and delay effective treatment. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: The perimenopause carries a genuinely increased risk of depressive symptoms and of a first depressive episode, with the risk concentrated in the years of most erratic hormonal fluctuation rather than after periods cease. This creates a diagnostic trap in both directions: attributing a major depressive episode to hormones and treating only with hormone therapy, or dismissing the hormonal context entirely and missing vasomotor symptoms that are themselves disrupting sleep and mood. Oestrogen therapy has evidence for depressive symptoms arising in perimenopause, particularly where vasomotor symptoms are prominent, but it is not established treatment for a major depressive episode, which is managed as it would be at any other time of life. Untreated depression in midlife carries the same risks of chronicity, relapse and suicide as at any other age, and women in this group are under treated relative to their symptom burden.
key_points: Depressive risk peaks during erratic hormonal fluctuation, not after menopause
Perimenopause is diagnosed clinically from cycle change and vasomotor symptoms
Gonadotrophins fluctuate and do not guide treatment in a woman over 45
A major depressive episode is treated on its own terms in this context
Hormone therapy addresses vasomotor symptoms and may assist mood alongside
explanation.pearls: Vasomotor symptoms that wake a woman several times a night are themselves a treatable driver of daytime mood and concentration, so treating them improves depression outcomes even when an antidepressant is the primary treatment.

sources.label: Australasian Menopause Society: Mood and menopause
RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders

subtopic_detail: Adolescent brought in after inhaling solvent from a bag with a perioral rash and new unsteadiness between episodes
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15 year old boy brought in by his aunt, who is his carer. She found him last night behind the shed with a plastic bag and a can of spray paint, and says this is the fourth time in two months.

He tells you it makes everything feel far away for about twenty minutes and that his friends do it too. His aunt says that in the past few weeks he has been dropping things, his handwriting has changed, and his teachers report he seems slower. He has not used alcohol or other drugs and has never been in trouble with police.

data_table.Examination: Erythematous scaling rash around the mouth and nostrils, mild bilateral hand tremor, intention tremor on finger to nose testing with past pointing, broad based unsteady gait, no nystagmus, power and reflexes normal, no hepatomegaly, mental state examination shows no psychotic features and no depressive episode
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, creatine kinase and venous blood gas all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Prescribe a benzodiazepine taper to manage withdrawal from the inhaled substance
options.rationale: Medically assisted withdrawal is the standard approach for alcohol and benzodiazepine dependence, where an abstinence syndrome is dangerous. Volatile substance withdrawal is mild and largely behavioural, and there is no established pharmacotherapy, so a benzodiazepine adds sedation without benefit. (Source: NSW Health: Volatile substance use)

options.text: Engage him and his carer, address the neurological signs, and involve youth services
options.rationale: Volatile substance use in a young person is managed through engagement, harm reduction and addressing the social context rather than through pharmacotherapy, because it is strongly associated with disadvantage, disengagement from school and unmet need rather than with dependence in the classical sense. The new cerebellar signs are the urgent element, since chronic solvent exposure causes a dose related and potentially irreversible leukoencephalopathy, and they require neurological assessment and imaging alongside the psychosocial work. (Source: NSW Health: Volatile substance use)

options.text: Reassure the family that this is experimental behaviour and review him in three months
options.rationale: Isolated experimentation without features of harm can reasonably be managed with education and review, and most adolescents who try a solvent do not continue. Repeated use over two months with new neurological signs has already crossed from experimentation into harm. (Source: NSW Health: Volatile substance use)

options.text: Report the matter to police so that supply of the product can be restricted
options.rationale: Supply restriction at the retail level is a genuine population level strategy and some jurisdictions restrict sales of certain products. A criminal justice response to an individual adolescent damages engagement, and volatile substance use itself is managed as a health issue in Australian policy. (Source: NSW Health: Volatile substance use)

options.text: Arrange an urgent electroencephalogram to investigate the episodes of detachment
options.rationale: Electroencephalography would be appropriate if the episodes of altered awareness were unexplained, stereotyped and not temporally tied to an exposure. Each episode here begins with inhalation and lasts about twenty minutes, which is the expected pharmacological course rather than a seizure. (Source: NSW Health: Volatile substance use)

explanation.summary: Volatile substance use, involving solvents, aerosols, glues, fuels and butane, is concentrated in young adolescents because the products are cheap, legal and universally available, and prevalence is markedly higher in communities experiencing disadvantage. The acute effect is a brief euphoric disinhibited state with a risk of sudden sniffing death from catecholamine sensitisation of the myocardium, which can occur on a first exposure and is precipitated by sudden exertion or fright. Chronic exposure to toluene containing products produces cerebellar and white matter damage with ataxia, tremor and cognitive decline, along with renal tubular acidosis and hearing loss, and these are dose related and only partly reversible. Management is a health and social response built on engagement, harm reduction, addressing schooling, housing and family circumstances, and neurological assessment where signs have emerged, since no pharmacotherapy exists.
key_points: Products are cheap, legal and universally available, so use starts young
Sudden sniffing death can occur on a first exposure with exertion or fright
A perioral rash is a useful physical clue to recent repeated use
Chronic toluene exposure causes cerebellar and white matter damage
Management is psychosocial and harm reduction based with no pharmacotherapy
explanation.pearls: Sudden sniffing death is precipitated by a surge of catecholamines during or just after inhalation, which is why anyone approaching an intoxicated young person should stay calm and avoid startling or chasing them.

subtopic_detail: Adolescent with long standing distress about their developing body and a consistently stated cross sex identity presenting with self harm
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 15 year old who was assigned female at birth, attending with a supportive mother. They tell you they have felt since early primary school that they are a boy, have asked to be called Sam for two years, and that since their chest developed they bind daily and avoid showering or swimming.

They have cut their forearms four times in the past six weeks, describing it as relief from distress rather than an attempt to die, and say they feel hopeless about what their body is becoming. They are attending school, have two close friends, and their mother asks you what you can do and where they should go.

data_table.Examination: Four superficial healed linear scars on the left forearm with no active wounds, no signs of constriction injury to the chest wall on examination with air entry equal and full, Tanner stage 4, mental state examination shows distress about body but no psychotic features, no current plan or intent to end life, protective factors include supportive mother and engaged schooling
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid stimulating hormone all within normal limits

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence testosterone after discussion of the risks and benefits with the family
options.rationale: Gender affirming hormone treatment is an appropriate consideration for some adolescents and it is prescribed in Australia within specialist services after multidisciplinary assessment. Initiating it from general practice at a first consultation bypasses the assessment, consent and endocrine processes that Australian standards require. (Source: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents)
source_refs: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.text: Treat the self harm with a psychological referral and set the gender question aside
options.rationale: Psychological support for self harm is unquestionably needed and is part of the plan. Separating it from the gender related distress that the young person identifies as its driver addresses the behaviour while leaving its cause unaddressed, and adolescents commonly disengage when that happens. (Source: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents)
source_refs: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.text: Advise waiting until 18 years before any assessment, with review appointments meanwhile
options.rationale: Delaying assessment until adulthood is sometimes framed as a cautious neutral position, but it is not neutral, because irreversible pubertal development continues during the wait. Australian standards support assessment and support during adolescence rather than deferral. (Source: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents)
source_refs: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.text: Refer for family therapy to address the mother's response to the disclosure
options.rationale: Family work is valuable where a young person faces rejection or conflict at home, and family support is one of the strongest protective factors in this group. This mother is already supportive and actively seeking help, so directing the intervention at her misplaces the need. (Source: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents)
source_refs: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

options.text: Refer to a specialist gender service while providing safety planning and support
options.rationale: A persistent, consistent and insistent cross gender identity since childhood with escalating distress at pubertal development warrants referral to a specialist multidisciplinary gender service, which is where assessment and any decisions about affirming treatment are made in Australia. The general practitioner's concurrent role is substantial and immediate, covering safety planning for the self harm, advice on safe chest binding to prevent skin and rib injury, use of the young person's name and pronouns, and being the continuing point of contact during what are often long waits. (Source: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents)
source_refs: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents

explanation.summary: Gender dysphoria describes clinically significant distress arising from incongruence between experienced gender and sex assigned at birth, and in adolescence it commonly intensifies with the physical changes of puberty. Trans and gender diverse young people have markedly elevated rates of self harm, suicidal ideation and depression compared with their peers, and the evidence consistently identifies family acceptance, use of chosen name and pronouns, and access to care as protective. Australian care operates through specialist multidisciplinary services that combine mental health, paediatric and endocrine expertise, with decisions about pubertal suppression or hormone treatment made within that framework rather than in primary care. The general practitioner's role is nonetheless central, providing continuity, safety planning, practical harm reduction such as binding advice, and management of coexisting mental illness during waits that are frequently measured in many months.
key_points: Distress typically escalates with the physical changes of puberty
Self harm and suicidality are markedly elevated in this group
Family acceptance and affirmed name use are strongly protective
Assessment and affirming treatment occur within specialist services
Deferring assessment is not neutral because puberty continues meanwhile
explanation.pearls: Daily chest binding with restrictive materials causes skin breakdown, back and chest pain and rib changes, so asking directly about binding practice and advising on a properly fitted binder worn for limited hours is a concrete harm reduction step available at the first consultation.

sources.label: RCH: Australian standards of care for trans and gender diverse children and adolescents
RACGP: Trans and gender diverse health

subtopic_detail: Low mood and tearfulness clearly tied to a recent redundancy with retained enjoyment and fleeting thoughts that life is not worth living
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 42 year old man made redundant seven weeks ago after nineteen years with the same employer. He describes feeling flattened and tearful, worrying constantly about the mortgage, and lying awake for an hour or two after going to bed.

He still enjoys watching his daughter play netball on Saturdays and went to a friend's fortieth last weekend and had a good night. His appetite and weight are unchanged and he wakes at his usual time. He tells you that once or twice he has thought his family would be better off without him, that the thought frightens him, that he would never act on it because of his children, and that he has no plan and has never self harmed. He asks you directly for antidepressants because a friend found them helpful.

data_table.Examination: Tearful when discussing work but engages and smiles when describing his daughter, no psychomotor retardation, speech normal in rate and form, no psychotic features, cognition intact, no signs of alcohol withdrawal and no stigmata of chronic liver disease
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function, thyroid stimulating hormone and glucose all within normal limits, alcohol intake by structured questioning is 6 standard drinks per week

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Safety planning with structured psychological therapy and early planned review
options.rationale: Symptoms proportionate to an identifiable stressor within three months, with preserved enjoyment, intact appetite and weight and no early morning waking, describe an adjustment disorder rather than a major depressive episode, and psychological therapy with practical problem solving is the evidence based treatment. Passive thoughts of being a burden still require an explicit safety plan and early review, because adjustment disorder carries a real suicide risk despite not meeting depressive criteria. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Start an antidepressant today as he has requested and review him in four weeks
options.rationale: Acceding to a clear patient request has value and antidepressants would be appropriate if he met criteria for a depressive episode. Evidence does not support antidepressants for adjustment disorder, and prescribing here exposes him to adverse effects, discontinuation problems and a diagnostic label that may affect insurance, without expected benefit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer him urgently to the acute mental health team for same day assessment
options.rationale: Urgent assessment is indicated for active suicidal intent, a formed plan, access to means with expressed intent, or psychotic depression. Fleeting ego dystonic thoughts that frighten him, with strong protective factors and no plan or intent, do not meet that threshold and an emergency response may deter future disclosure. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Prescribe a short course of a hypnotic for his sleep and review in one month
options.rationale: His sleep onset difficulty is real and hypnotics would shorten it in the short term. They do not address the worry driving the insomnia, carry dependence risk, and are specifically discouraged where suicidal thoughts are present because of overdose potential. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Reassure him that this is a normal reaction and review him only if things worsen
options.rationale: Normalising his reaction is a reasonable and important part of the conversation, since distress after redundancy is expected. Symptoms that have persisted seven weeks with impairment and passive suicidal thoughts warrant active treatment and scheduled follow up rather than open ended watchful waiting. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

explanation.summary: Adjustment disorder is an emotional or behavioural response to an identifiable stressor beginning within three months of it, causing distress out of proportion to what would be expected or significant functional impairment, and not meeting criteria for another disorder. The distinction from a major depressive episode rests on the biological features and on pervasiveness, since preserved reactivity of mood, normal appetite and weight and absence of early morning waking all argue against a depressive episode. This distinction matters because treatment differs: psychological therapy and practical problem solving have evidence in adjustment disorder while antidepressants do not, and prescribing them conveys risk without expected benefit. Suicide risk is nonetheless substantial in adjustment disorder and is not proportional to the diagnostic label, so safety planning and scheduled review are required whenever thoughts of death are disclosed.
key_points: Onset is within three months of an identifiable stressor
Preserved enjoyment, appetite and sleep pattern argue against a depressive episode
Psychological therapy and problem solving are the evidence based treatment
Antidepressants lack evidence for adjustment disorder specifically
Suicide risk is real and requires safety planning regardless of the label
explanation.pearls: Adjustment disorder is over represented among people who die by suicide relative to how mild the diagnosis sounds, with the act often occurring impulsively and close to the stressor, which is why means restriction and a written safety plan belong in the first consultation.

sources.label: RANZCP: Clinical practice guidelines for mood disorders
